Jurisdiction: anonymised, but facts: 2008 executive order requiring SRS for gender marker change on national ID; 90% blocked; health ministry recognises self-determination as human right since 2013 but surgery requirement stands; Aug 2024 court refused marker change without surgery; appeal indicated, unresolved. Rising anti-gender movement, one party "two genders"; pending conscription changes. But: pride marches large (170,000), trans march 3,000, described as most progressive in region, education anti-discrimination law, employment anti-discrimination, conversion therapy banned, same-sex adoption, sodomy legal, open public expression.

Crucially for a visitor: the surgery requirement is a resident-facing LGR issue — a visitor uses their home passport. Per rubric rule 1, LGR is climate signal, not a direct traveler protection or exposure. No documented border/entry restrictions for trans visitors. No documented trans-specific violence, no hate crime data. No police targeting documented. Facilities: gender-neutral bathrooms limited but expanding; 17% discrimination in restrooms — that's a documented social friction/hostility in facilities, but that statistic is trans-specific survey (though population/methodology unclear — it's "trans and gender-neutral survey respondents who reported discrimination"). That's an everyday-exposure signal but modest; and bathroom access isn't a legal ban on trans people using facilities — no bathroom bill documented. Government is actively expanding gender-neutral facilities. Some mismatch: only 5/149 meet standards — implementation gap.

Social climate: rising anti-gender movement, but also large pride, legal protections in education/employment, conversion therapy ban, adoption. Described as most progressive in region.

So what's the traveler-facing picture? Document mismatch risk at airport security if a visitor's passport marker doesn't match presentation — but that's the visitor's home documents; no documented friction by border officials here. No criminalisation of gender expression. No documented police harassment of trans visitors. Society: broadly tolerant with a noisy anti-gender minority; some restroom friction.

This resembles the 0.75–0.85 tier. Let me consider: 0.85 anchors describe strong protections with functioning remedies for visitors. This dossier has no documented remedies operating for trans visitors specifically; no documented trans-specific hate crime law covering GI (education/employment protections are resident-facing, not visitor remedies). Actually the employment anti-discrimination is resident-facing. Rule of law appears functional, civil society strong, courts issue rulings (against trans claimant, but functioning).

Absence of resident-facing machinery is not a deduction. Missing hate-crime statute is a resident gap — light.

Documented negatives reaching visitors: restroom/changing-room discrimination (17% of reported discrimination) — societal friction/hostility in facilities, tier 2-3-ish, but no state-imposed facility exclusion. No documented trans-specific violence. No documented border friction. Anti-gender movement is a climate signal raising risk of hostility slightly.

Also: no documented instance of targeted screening; explicitly unresolved.

So the worst documented feature is tier 3-ish/4: societal friction in restrooms (a minority of respondents), rising anti-gender rhetoric. No state-imposed universal exposure reaching visitors (the surgery requirement doesn't reach visitors' documents). Conscription changes are resident-facing for minors? Conscription applies to citizens, not visitors.

Minors: a trans minor travelling with a guardian — no entry restrictions documented; education anti-discrimination covers schools but a visitor minor wouldn't enroll. No conversion therapy risk documented (banned). No family-based risk documented.

So rating around 0.70–0.78. Compare to 0.75-C (Meridia: passports may bear matching marker, trained border officers, tribunal hears appeals, brief detention, wide officer discretion, uneven airport practice) — that has documented protections for travelers: trained border officers, tribunal. Here we lack documented traveler-facing protections but also lack documented traveler-facing harms. 0.75-D (Alderland: equality statute protecting visitors, police intervene, but violence in nightlife, uncertainty) — that's more documented.

0.65-A/B: documented incident with remedy working. This dossier has no documented travel incidents at all; it's a thin-data-on-visitors situation, but a rich documented record of institutions: courts functioning, anti-discrimination laws, conversion therapy ban, huge pride attendance, government investment in gender-neutral facilities. That plus absence of any documented visitor-facing restriction or targeted violence pushes above 0.65. But the unresolved items (documents at entry, no hate crime recourse, rising anti-gender movement, restroom friction) keep it below 0.85. Also the marker-change refusal shows the state's highest court-level institutions denying trans claims — that's a climate signal lowering it somewhat (hostility in institutions on trans-specific questions), though the 2017 constitutional interpretation protected orientation.

Also the 2018 referendum banning LGBT-inclusive sex education — a state-backed setback, indicating social majority conservatism on trans issues. But 170,000 pride attendance by 2019 suggests large liberal segment.

I'd place ~0.72–0.75. Let me pick 0.74? Hmm. Let's consider the anchor instruction: compare to at least three anchors. 0.75-C has documented traveler-facing protections and known friction; our jurisdiction has no documented traveler-layer at all — an open question — but strong general institutional climate. Per rule 13, open questions are light; absence of resident machinery lightest; a known traveler-facing exposure heaviest. Here the known exposure reaching visitors: some restroom/changing-room discrimination (documented, trans-specific survey, moderate), rising anti-gender hostility (climate). That's roughly 0.70–0.75.

I'll go 0.72.
